h: Kings, Sieges and a Saxon Church
p: The Great Tower was built for Henry II in the 1180s, one of the most impressive keeps of its age, and the interiors have been dressed to show how the king's court might have looked, with colourful furnishings and bustling scenes. In 1216, the castle held out against a long siege by the French prince Louis, a dramatic moment that helped save the English crown. The castle was later strengthened again and again as threats changed over the centuries.

Right next to the Roman lighthouse stands the Saxon church of St Mary in Castro, a wonderful old survivor that still feels peaceful amid all the battlements. It's easy to walk past, so make a point of popping in.

Much of the castle's later fame comes from the Second World War. In May 1940, Vice Admiral Bertram Ramsay masterminded Operation Dynamo, the evacuation of Allied troops from Dunkirk, from the tunnels beneath the castle. It's an extraordinary story to stand so close to.

Afterwards, head for the White Cliffs, where National Trust paths lead along the clifftops towards South Foreland Lighthouse. Dover Museum in the town centre is home to the Dover Bronze Age Boat, a remarkable survivor more than 3,000 years old. For a quieter seaside stop, Samphire Hoe, created from material dug out for the Channel Tunnel, is a lovely spot below the cliffs, while Deal and Walmer castles are a short drive up the coast.
